lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: The Last Sermon of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W)
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

The lesson is about the migration and teachings of the Holy Prophet (S.A.W). Born in 571 AD at Makkah in a respected Quraish family, he asked the Quraish to worship the One true God. Most refused, thinking he was against their gods and their ancestors, and opposed him. He migrated to Yathrib in 622 AD. The day he entered Yathrib marks the start of the Islamic calendar. He stopped first at Quba, outside the city, and built a mosque there. Yathrib was renamed Madinat un-Nabi, then shortened to Madina.

Key Points

  • In Madina he drew up the Charter of Madina, united the Arab tribes under Islam, and carried out social and religious reforms.
  • The Charter covered the rights and duties of Muslims and Jews, freedom of religion, and no alliance with outside enemies; disputes were referred to the Prophet (S.A.W).
  • Groups in Madina: Muslims, pagans, hypocrites and Jews.
  • His farewell pilgrimage in the 10th year of Hijra was his first and last Hajj; he taught how to perform Hajj and delivered the Last Sermon in the Uranah valley of Mount Arafat.

Messages of the Last Sermon

  • Hurt no one, so you may not be hurt in return.
  • Men and women have rights over each other.
  • All Muslims are tied in the bond of brotherhood; life and property of every Muslim are a sacred trust.
  • No Arab is superior to a non-Arab and no white to a black except by piety and good action; all mankind is from Adam, who was created from dust.
  • Return things kept in trust to their owners; beware of Satan in small matters; carry these words to those who are absent.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
ancestorsforefathers
migratemove to another place to live
hypocritespeople who claim belief but do not truly believe
pagansidol worshippers
harmonypeaceful agreement
prohibitedforbidden
pietyGod-fearing goodness
equitablefair and just

Remember

Following the messages of the Last Sermon builds a fair and equitable society based on honesty, justice and merit, so that all people get their fair share.

lessons.title: Listening and Speaking: Sharing Information and Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 1.2 Listening and Speaking has the focus: Sharing information and ideas. Exercise 1 says all students must listen to what others are saying and participate fully in the discussion. The whole activity is about unfair means in exams, linking speaking practice to the unit theme of ethics and character building.

How to Work

  • Step A: Work in groups of 4-5, as instructed by the teacher. Discuss one topic from the list, as assigned by the teacher. Select two members who should note all the points discussed. Make sure everyone takes part.
  • Step B: Prepare a presentation. Compile all the ideas discussed, decide which member will say what, and decide the order in which members will speak.
  • Step C: At the end of the presentation, each group should ask the class to suggest any point they might have missed. The note takers should note these points.

Topics

No.Discussion topic
1Some unfair means that students use in exams
2Reasons for using unfair means in exams
3Impact of using unfair means in exams on students' performance
4Effect of using unfair means on the future of students

Remember

Finally, collect all the data and prepare a talk for giving in the assembly, to discourage use of unfair means during exams. Listening carefully, noting points and letting everyone speak are the skills this section teaches.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Second Conditional Sentences
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Type 2 (second) conditional sentences are often used for talking about imaginary or unreal situations. You learnt Type 1 in earlier classes; here you practise Type 2.

  • The verb in the clause with 'if' is in the simple past or past continuous tense.
  • The verb in the other clause uses the modal 'would' (negative 'wouldn't'); 'could' and 'might' and their negatives can also be used.
  • The 'if' clause can come at the beginning or at the end.
  • The 'if' clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.
  • In a Type 2 'if' clause, sometimes 'were' is used instead of 'was'.

Examples

ExamplePoint shown
If they drank sufficient water, they would have a healthy skin.if + past, would
If Sana was watching television, the lights would be on.past continuous in if-clause
I would go mad, if I received a billion rupees.if-clause at the end
If allowed, they could sleep the whole day.could in main clause

Key Points

Correct matches include: If all people in Pakistan became honest, the country would progress very fast; If money grew on trees, everyone would be rich; If she studied harder, she would get better marks; People would fly, if they had wings; If I owned a camera, I would take many photographs.

Remember

Pattern: If + past simple, ... would / could / might + base verb. The situation is imagined, not real.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is imaginary or unreal situations, because the book says Type 2 conditionals are often used for talking about imaginary or unreal situations.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is simple past or past continuous, because that is the first rule printed for second conditional sentences.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Punctuation
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

This Language Practice task asks you to correct the punctuation and capitalization in a passage about forming habits. The corrected opening is: 'How long does it take to form a new habit? I looked for an answer the same way most people do nowadays. I asked Google. The answer I got was 21 days.'

Grammar Rules

  • Put a capital letter at the start of every sentence.
  • Use capitals for I, and for proper names such as Google, Mr Mohan and Multan University.
  • End statements with full stops and questions with question marks.
  • Use commas in lists, for example: exercise, smoking, writing a diary, or turning cartwheels.
  • Use commas before clauses where needed.
  • Use apostrophes in contractions such as didn't and weren't.

Key Points

MarkUse in this passage
Capital letterSentence start; I; Google; Mr Mohan; Multan University
Full stopEnd of a statement
Question markEnd of a question, such as the opening habit question
CommaIn lists and before clauses where needed
ApostropheIn didn't and weren't

Remember

Check every sentence in order: capital at the start, correct end mark, commas in lists, and apostrophes where letters are missing in contractions.

lessons.title: Writing: Descriptive Essay and Formal Letters
lessons.notes_html:
Descriptive Essay: How to Write

In the model essay about deserts, the thesis statement is given in one sentence at the end of the introductory paragraph, pointing to the remarkable Sahara Desert. A topic sentence opens each body paragraph and the idea is then explained with facts and examples. Body paragraph 1: springs of water are few and far apart in deserts. Body paragraph 2: the Sahara is one of the most remarkable deserts in the world. The closing paragraph begins with the signalling phrase 'To conclude', briefly gathers the main points and ends with a general concluding idea.

Model Essay: My Village

My village is a small, green and peaceful place where everyone knows one another. Its fields, trees and simple homes make it a lovely place to live. The village has one main street, a small market, a mosque and a school. The people are kind, hardworking and always ready to help. In the morning the fields look fresh and the birds sing in the trees. In the evening children play in the open ground while elders sit and talk. I love my village because it is clean, calm and full of love. Essay topics offered: My village / town / city; A historical place; A scenic place; School playground, in at least four paragraphs.

Formal Letters: Letters to the Editor

  • First model letter: to The Editor of the Daily Dawn, Karachi, addressed 'Dear Sir', about traffic accidents.
  • Second model letter: to The Editor of the Express Tribune, Karachi, addressed 'Dear Madam', about plastic bags and the harm they cause, written by Munir Altaf of Turbat.
  • The first writer signed as 'A Concerned Citizen' of Multan, so no personal name is given.
  • Both letters give reasons and both give suggestions.

How to Write a Letter to the Editor

ParagraphContent
1State the problem
2Give reasons for the problem
3Give suggestions

Model topic from the builder: Shortage of Clean Drinking Water, with reasons of old and broken pipes, wastage of water and tanks not cleaned, and suggestions to repair pipes, clean tanks regularly and start an awareness drive.

lessons.title: Study Skills: Editing
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Study Skills: Editing means finding and correcting errors in a written text, including wrong pronouns, wrong verb forms, wrong words, missing words and punctuation. Unit 1 practises this on two stories: The Wise King and The Four Seasons.

Key Points: The Wise King

  • Correct 'her sons' to 'his sons'; 'after his death. When he died' needs a full stop and capital W.
  • One son found a vessel full of pearls, another gold and silver coins, the fourth a vessel full of bones, and the first a vessel full of dust.
  • The king decided the one with dust was to get all the land, and the owner of the cattle was decided likewise; all the brothers were pleased, amazed at the king's wisdom, satisfied and happy.

Key Points: The Four Seasons

ParagraphNumber of errorsExamples of corrections
First5four sons (not son); sent (not send); great distance (not greet)
Second10in spring (not on spring); had seen (not see); third son (not three son); drooping (not dropping)
Third5the tree's life (not trees life); told them (not tell); Don't with an apostrophe

Remember

The Four Seasons has twenty errors in total: five in the first paragraph, ten in the second and five in the third. The father's lesson is not to judge life by only one season, since each son had seen only one season of the pear tree's life.

lessons.title: Fun: Travel Brochure
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 1.6 Fun is for having fun with language and is not to be formally assessed. The activity is a Travel brochure. Work in groups of four. Each group represents a travel agent. Your job is to prepare a travel brochure to attract people to visit a particular place. A brochure is a kind of pamphlet that gives brief information about a programme, place, activity, etc. The group that develops the best brochure, a colourful brochure with good, brief information, will be the winner.

How to Write: Step 1

  • Think of a place that you want people to visit.
  • Brainstorm: why should people visit that place, what is nice and attractive about it; what will people need to take with them; what are the modes of travel they can use, i.e. train, bus, car, plane, etc.; what are some things they must see, eat, buy, etc.; what are some important things to remember.

How to Write: Step 2

  • Discuss and decide a name for your travel agency.
  • Think about what your brochure will look like: the shape of the brochure, how you would write the information, the pictures or drawings you will use, etc.
  • Decide who will do what, for example who will collect the information and pictures, who will write or draw, etc.
  • Start developing the brochure.

Remember

Winning brochureFeatures
Best brochureColourful, with good and brief information
Group sizeFour students, acting as a travel agent

Brochures made in class are displayed in the class or school.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Shah Abdul Latif
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 2, Role Model, presents the life of Shah Abdul Latif, the great saint and poet of Sindh, as a role model. The lesson covers his life in seven aspects, so read it aspect by aspect and note the main point of each one.

Summary: The Seven Aspects

No.AspectKey Point
1Background and FamilyHis forefather migrated to Sindh from Afghanistan.
2The Name BhitaiHe is called Bhitai because he spent a good part of his life on a mound (a bhit).
3Early Life and EducationHe loved studying and had a command over other languages.
4YouthHe was married for a short period of time only.
5Spiritual GrowthHe found pleasure in praying, thinking and devotion.
6Death and RemembranceA shrine was built over his grave sometime after his death.
7Shah Latif's PoetryHis poetry is mainly about Sindh, but other places are also mentioned.

Key Points

  • He left home in 1742 and lived on a mound (Bhit) for the rest of his life, so he is called the Saint of Bhit.
  • Information about his early life was collected from oral traditions: Mirza Kalich Beg gathered details from old people who had heard them from their fathers and grandfathers. It was collected in this manner because his life had mostly survived through oral tradition, not written records.
  • He knew Arabic and Persian quite well, and he had deep knowledge of the Holy Qur'an and the Hadiths.
  • His collection included the works of Moulana Jalaluddin Rumi (the Masnavi) and Shah Karim.
  • He is known for two skills: composing poetry and spiritual devotion (mysticism).
  • At his Urs, people gather and listen to the saint's songs sung on the Tambooro, and learned men read papers about his life and poetry.
  • His ancestors migrated to Sindh to gain spiritual contact with Bilawal, a pious man, and because they liked Sindh, then a centre of Muslim culture.
  • After his wife died he did not marry again, because his heart turned more and more towards religion and devotion; he felt restless and found a normal domestic life difficult.
  • People became his followers because his spiritual power grew through prayer and devotion, and they were strongly impressed by his gentle ways.
  • Places named in his poetry include Istanbul, Samarkand, Rome, Kabul, Kandahar, Delhi, Deccan, China, the Malabar coast, Sri Lanka and Java, because his poems describe Sindhi sailors and their voyages.
  • The Risalo has been translated into English and Urdu.
  • His key message is acceptable to everyone because his spiritual poetry carries a message of love, which is universal. We can practise it today through love, tolerance, kindness and care for others.

About the Text

Key Points: How Exercise 1 Works

  • Work in groups of six.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Modals for Ability
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

The modal verbs are can, could, may, might, shall, should, will and would. Modals are used for different language functions, like talking about ability, asking permission, making requests and giving suggestions. In this unit we learn to use can, could and may for ability and permission.

Ability

  • We use can to talk about someone's skill or general abilities at a given time in the present or future: He can swim like a fish. They can't speak Punjabi very well. You can get good marks in the exams.
  • We use could to talk about past time: She could speak several languages. They couldn't write very well.
  • Negative forms: can + not = cannot / can't; could + not = could not / couldn't.
TimeAbleNot able
Present / futurecancannot (can't)
Pastcouldcould not (couldn't)

Permission

  • We also use can to ask for permission: Can I borrow your pencil, please? Can we go home now?
  • The use of could is more formal and polite than can: Could I borrow your pencil, please?
  • Another more formal and polite way of asking for permission is with may: May I borrow your pencil, please? May we go home now?
  • We use can to give permission: You can go home now if you like. We can also use may as a more formal and polite way of giving permission: You may go home now, if you like.

Writing About Your Own Abilities

Follow this pattern: When I was nine years old, I could ride a bicycle. But, I couldn't swim. Now, I can read English stories. However, I can't drive a car. When I grow up, I can become a famous doctor. In Dialogue A, can and could are used for ability (Zahra, Najma and Farah talk about speaking Chinese, Persian and Arabic). In Dialogue B, can, could and may are used for permission (Areeb asks his mother, 'Can I play now?' and 'May I take my new bicycle?').

Remember

Ask yourself two questions: Is it about the present or the past? Is it ability or permission? Present ability = can, past ability = could, and for polite permission use could or may.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Suffixes
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules: What Is a Suffix?

We sometimes add a pair or group of alphabets at the end of a word to add something to the meaning of a word. These are called suffixes. We can use suffixes to make many new words, including nouns. In this unit we learn three noun suffixes: ment, ness and al.

Book Examples

Word + SuffixNew WordSuffix
agree + mentagreementment
postpone + mentpostponementment
willing + nesswillingnessness
frank + nessfranknessness
arrive + alarrivalal
profession + alprofessionalal

Key Points: Nouns with ment

  • judge + ment = judgement (given as the example: As soon as the judgement was given, the reporters left the court room.)
  • treat + ment = treatment: Zaman is back to work after his treatment.
  • pay + ment = payment: The workers receive their weekly payment every Friday.
  • employ + ment = employment: My son is looking for employment as he lost his job last week.
  • retire + ment = retirement: After his retirement at the age of sixty he has decided to write a book.
  • manage + ment = management: The management of the school announced their new admission policy yesterday.

Key Points: Nouns with ness

  • ill + ness = illness: Her illness has made her weak.
  • soft + ness = softness: I love the softness of our new sofa set.
  • bold + ness = boldness: Our neighbour's son, who is a soldier, fought the enemy with boldness.
  • kind + ness = kindness: The principal of our school treats everyone with kindness.
  • neat + ness = neatness: My mother taught us neatness in all our work.

Key Points: Nouns with al

  • survive + al = survival: The survival of the green turtle is in danger on the Karachi beaches.
  • propose + al = proposal: Our proposal for setting up a dispensary was accepted by the minister.
  • remove + al = removal: The removal of garbage is the responsibility of the government.
  • sign + al = signal: The train moved out of the station as soon as the guard gave the signal.
  • approve + al = approval: I needed my parents' approval for going to friend's wedding.

Remember

First decide which noun fits the meaning of the sentence, then add the right suffix to its base word: ment after verbs like employ, treat, pay, retire, manage and judge; ness after adjectives like ill, bold, neat, kind and soft; al after verbs like survive, propose, remove, sign and approve.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is treatment, because treat + ment makes the noun treatment, which fits the sentence about Zaman returning to work after being treated.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is illness, because ill + ness makes the noun illness, and the suffix ness is added to the adjective ill in this exercise.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is boldness, because bold + ness makes the noun boldness, which describes the brave quality with which the soldier fought.

lessons.title: Writing: Narrative Essay and Summary Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Narrative Essay: What It Is

A narrative essay is focused on telling a story. It includes important details about the incident. When writing a narrative essay, include details about: when and where the event or incident took place; what happened, including significant details; and what is its significance at the personal, societal and country level.

How to Write a Narrative Essay

  • Choose a story that is about the topic or theme that you have been assigned or you have chosen.
  • Make an outline of the plot before you begin; this will help you put your story in order.
  • Describe the important characters such that people can see them.
  • Describe the setting in a manner that the readers feel that they are seeing the scene.
  • Usually, the third person, i.e. he, she, it, is used along with common and proper nouns (boy, Salim).
  • Make sure your theme is clearly illustrated in the story.
  • Keep the readers' interest and attention, and leave the reader with something to think about.

Steps for Writing (Exercise 3)

  • Brainstorm; select a topic for the essay, based on the story selected; decide why you want to tell that story; select the points and ideas that you want to include.
  • Prepare an outline of the story; be clear about the order in which you plan to tell the story and how you want to conclude it.
  • Write the introductory paragraph, giving the background and purpose; narrate the incident; relate the incident to the purpose; write the concluding paragraph.
  • Edit your work for organization of ideas, correctness of grammar and punctuation, and appropriate introductory and concluding paragraphs.

The Model Story: Two Brothers

Tanveer and Junaid were twin brothers who looked exactly alike but were quite different in nature: Junaid always thought carefully before doing anything, while Tanveer did things without thinking. Their father had saved enough money to buy only one of them a bicycle, so he set up a competition: both would set out right after the morning prayers, walk as far as each could, and return by sunset; the one who completed the task would get the prize. Tanveer sprinted off, ran far ahead to the end of the town and further, grew very tired, and returned long after sunset. Junaid walked until midday, turned around, and returned home in time. Junaid won because he completed the task according to instructions; Tanveer lost because he had not returned within the time. The lesson Tanveer learnt was to think before doing things. In the model essay written as Tanveer's teacher, the writer explains the reason for the competition, states what Tanveer did and why, describes what his brother did, explains who won and why, identifies Tanveer's mistakes (rushing, ignoring the time limit, acting without thought), and expresses regret and the wish that Tanveer should slow down and plan first.

Summary Writing: Do's and Don'ts

Do'sDon'ts
Include all the main ideas.Do not reproduce sentences from the original text.
Select points from all the paragraphs.Do not repeat any point or idea.
Limit your summary by not including all the details.Do not introduce new ideas.
Use simple, short sentences.Do not criticise.
Link sections and points with appropriate linking words.Do not change anything given in the original text; do not give your own opinion.

Summary Example: Moen-jo-Daro

First underline the main ideas and words in each paragraph, without details, then use those key words to write the summary. The model summary says: Moen-jo-Daro in Sindh was one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, which developed around 3000 BC in areas that today form Pakistan and North India; the city, one of the oldest in the world, was built around 2600 BC; it remained unknown until 1922, when villagers found old pots and bricks and Sir John Marshall ordered digging; the digging revealed a well-planned city of straight roads, baked-brick houses with bathrooms, covered drains and shops; its people were traders, farmers and skilled craftsmen who lived a rich, happy life; how they ended is unknown, perhaps a raid from the north or a great earthquake.

lessons.title: Study Skills: Editing Practice
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 2.5 Study Skills is for acquiring additional language skills and is not to be formally assessed. It gives editing practice. There are many types of activities that can help sharpen our editing skills. One such activity is the C-test.

Key Points: The C-Test

  • In this activity incomplete words have to be completed by using the context for clues to guess what the word might be.
  • In the passage 'The Duties of a Good Citizen', beginning from the second word of the second sentence, half or sometimes half plus one extra letters have been removed from every second word.
  • Work in pairs and first orally complete all the words. Once you have done so, write the complete passage in your notebook.
  • Rule from the teacher's note: if a word has an even number of letters, i.e. 4, 6, 8, etc., then half the letters would be missing in that word. However, if the word has an odd number of letters, i.e. 3, 5, 7, etc., then half the number plus one more letter would be missing. For example, the word 'tailor' will be written as tai___ and the word 'would' will be written as wo___.
  • Read the whole sentence, as this gives an idea of the context and makes it easier to guess the word.

The Duties of a Good Citizen: Completed Words

The completed passage begins: The milkman brings milk for us; the baker bakes the bread; the printer prints our books; the driver drives the bus in which we go to school or the place of work. The teacher teaches the pupils at school, the doctor treats the sick and the shopkeeper sells articles of daily use. The traffic policemen regulate the traffic so that we may travel without any fear of accident. We must repay society for all these gifts. If a milkman mixes water in the milk, how can he expect other members of society to treat him fairly? If we ignore traffic rules, we not only endanger the lives of others, but our own as well. It is our duty to be loyal and patriotic to Pakistan. We should pay our taxes promptly, fully and honestly, so that we may continue to enjoy all social benefits. Islam lays great stress on our duties as citizens.

Exercise 2: Editing a Passage

You are the editor of your school magazine. Work in pairs to edit the passage about students' duties. The corrections are:

WrongCorrect
there parenttheir parents
they must not becameThey must not become
fellow the standard disciplinefollow the standard discipline
establish a routine with studyingestablish a routine of studying
languachlanguage
towords every onetowards everyone
good that is unhealthyfood that is unhealthy

Remember

Editing means reading slowly, using the sense of the whole sentence, and fixing spelling, word choice and grammar: their (not there) for possession, follow (not fellow), language (not languach), towards everyone, and food that is unhealthy.

lessons.title: Fun: Recitation and Visual Presentation of a Poem
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Unit 2.6 Fun is for having fun with language and is not to be formally assessed. Its activity is the recitation and visual presentation of a poem. The poem given here is one of Shah Latif's poems, translated by Elsa Kazi.

The Poem: RAIN

The rain pours on the desert sands / On hills and vales around; / At early dawn we rise to hear, / The churns soft, humming sound-

The hands are full of butter, wives / With merriment abound- / Each buffalo for milking brought; / Athwart the grassy ground; / In thatches here we never found / Mistress and mind so glad!

Season's Orchestra's in full swing, / Fresh showers ease the mind; / On mountain-side so green with grass; / Cattle abundance find; / Gay herdsmen's wives about their necks / Of blossoms garlands wind;

Cucumbers, mushrooms, vegetables / Food of every kind; / Lord! Days of dearth let lie behind, / Ne'er let them reach the earth.

Key Points

  • Exercise 1: Work in groups of four and recite the poem. Each group should read one verse only.
  • The poem describes the joy of rain in the desert: rain on the sands, hills and vales, the humming sound of churns at dawn, hands full of butter, buffaloes brought for milking, green mountain-sides, cattle finding abundance, and plenty of food of every kind.
  • The last verse is a prayer: the days of dearth (shortage) should be left behind and never reach the earth again.
  • Exercise 2: Continue working in the same groups of four and draw the scene described in the verse that you recited, on a chart paper. Colour or paint the picture. Write the verse in beautiful and fancy writing on the chart.
  • All the charts will be displayed in the class and the group with the best drawing will be the winner.

Vocabulary from the Poem

WordMeaning in the Poem
valesvalleys, in 'hills and vales around'
churnsthe vessels whose soft, humming sound is heard at early dawn
merrimentjoy; the wives are full of merriment
aboundare plentiful; wives with merriment abound
abundanceplenty; cattle abundance find
dearthshortage; days of dearth are days of want

Remember

Recite your group's verse clearly and with feeling, then present the same verse visually: draw its scene, colour or paint it, and copy the verse in beautiful, fancy writing on the chart.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is abundance, because the verse says 'On mountain-side so green with grass; / Cattle abundance find.'

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: Chasing Dreams
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

In Chasing Dreams, Jameel and his sister Sara live in a village and dream of studying further and becoming doctors. There is no college in or near their village; the only college is 50 miles away in the city. With hard work, tuitions, family sacrifice and help from others, both study in the city, first at college and then at medical college. In the end Jameel builds a hospital in their village among green fields, and Sara guides village women in health and hygiene.

Key Points

  • Eleven people appear: six main characters - Jameel, Sara, Khalid, father, mother and Aunt Sadori - and five minor ones - Uncle Sarmad (mentioned), Allah Bachayo, Allah Dinno, Uncle Noor Ali and Jameel's wife.
  • Jameel was upset because it seemed impossible to continue his studies and become a doctor.
  • Sara hid her feelings because she did not want her father to know she was hurt that only Jameel was allowed to go to the city.
  • Both had to pass every test in the first go because the family had very little money and could not afford failure.
  • Expenses were managed by giving tuitions, and in the fourth year father and Khalid sold a big piece of fertile land to pay the fees.
  • Lessons: where there is a will there is a way; hard work and family sacrifice fulfil dreams; education is for both men and women; serve your own community.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
shabbyold and in poor condition
collapsedfell down suddenly
reluctantlyunwillingly
preoccupiedbusy thinking about something
obligatorynecessary, required by duty
siblingsbrothers and sisters
realizeto make something happen, to fulfil
weatheredworn by sun and wind, aged
impressivegrand, making a strong impression
backdropthe background scene
hostedarranged and held an event
bornecarried, endured

Remember

The family had dinner in the courtyard, around the table in front of the house. Sara had two young children, and the family travelled in a small jeep at the end of the story.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is eleven: six main characters and five minor characters appear in the story.

lessons.title: Listening and Speaking: Expressing Emotions and Wishes
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

Often, emotions and wishes are expressed by using the word wish. The book gives three main uses of wish.

Key Points

  • A desire for something not possible: Wish is most commonly used to express a desire for something which is not possible. Example: I wish you were here. (Unfortunately, you are not, and I miss you.)
  • Greetings and goodwill: Wish is also used in greetings and expressions of goodwill. Examples: We wish you a Happy Eid. Wish you a safe and pleasant journey.
  • Regret: Sometimes wish is used to express regret. Example: I wish you had done the work. (You did not do the work and I am annoyed because of that.)

Dialogue Practice

Work in pairs, take the roles of Student A and Student B, then change roles. In the dialogue, Student B says: Wish you a very happy birthday, and: I wish I had come. Student A ends with: Wish you a safe journey, for the trip to Islamabad tomorrow evening.

SituationWish
A friend's birthdayWish you a very happy birthday.
Eid dayWish you a happy Eid.
A friend cannot come to a weddingI wish you could come.
Poor marks in examsI wish I had got good marks.
A friend going to DubaiWish you a safe and pleasant journey.
Malaria from mosquitoesI wish I had protected myself from mosquitoes.

Remember

Choose the wish by its use: a greeting for a festival or journey, and I wish I had... for regret about the past.

options: A desire for something which is not possible
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a desire for something not possible, the most common use of wish given in the book.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Types of Sentences
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

In English we have different types of sentences. Each type is used for a specific purpose. This lesson teaches two types, each affirmative or negative.

  • Declarative sentences are generally called statements. They can be affirmative or negative. Examples: I am tired. / I am not tired. Raheel is hungry. / Raheel is not hungry. I have four pencils. / I do not have four pencils.
  • Interrogative sentences are question forms, used to make enquiries, to confirm information, and so on. They can be affirmative or negative. Examples: Are you hungry? / Are you not hungry? Did you do your homework? / Did you not do your homework?

Key Points

SentenceType
Sabiha is shivering.Declarative affirmative
The stranger was not calling from the hospital.Declarative negative
Are we going to the football field?Interrogative affirmative
Is this not your book? (Isn't this your book?)Interrogative negative
Juman does not like to play hockey.Declarative negative

How to Change Them

Change affirmative sentences into negative and negative ones into affirmative: Sabiha is not shivering. The stranger was calling from the hospital. With the key word book: Declarative affirmative - This book is very interesting. Declarative negative - This book is not very interesting. Interrogative affirmative - Is this book interesting? Interrogative negative - Is this book not interesting?

Remember

A statement ends with a full stop; a question ends with a question mark and contains a negative word like not when it is negative.

mcqs.q: What are declarative sentences generally called?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is statements, because declarative sentences are generally called statements in the book.

mcqs.q: What are interrogative sentences used for?
options: To make enquiries and confirm information
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to make enquiries and confirm information, which is the purpose of interrogative sentences.

mcqs.q: 'Sabiha is shivering' is which type?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is declarative affirmative, the example type given in the book for this statement.

mcqs.q: 'Are we going to the football field?' is which type?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is interrogative affirmative, because it is a question form with no negative word.

mcqs.q: 'The stranger was not calling from the hospital' is which type?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is declarative negative, because it is a statement containing the negative word not.

mcqs.q: 'Isn't this your book?' is which type?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is interrogative negative, because it is a question form containing the negative isn't.

mcqs.q: 'Juman doesn't like to play hockey' is which type?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is declarative negative, because it is a statement with the negative doesn't.

mcqs.q: Change 'Sabiha is shivering' into negative form.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Sabiha is not shivering, formed by adding not to make the affirmative statement negative.

mcqs.q: Change 'The stranger was not calling from the hospital' into affirmative form.
options: The stranger was calling from the hospital
The stranger was not calling again
mcqs.why: The correct answer is The stranger was calling from the hospital, formed by removing not from the negative statement.

mcqs.q: With key word book, which is interrogative negative?
options: This book is not very interesting.
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Isn't this book interesting, because it is a question form with the negative isn't.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Use of Articles A, An, The
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

Fill blanks with a, an, the, where necessary. Remember that a / an are used with countable singular nouns, and the is used in a number of places, for example: when referring to a particular thing, before superlative degrees, when using two comparative degrees together, before the names of rivers, seas, mountains, etc., before titles, nationalities, names of institutions, communities, and so on. The is also used for something already mentioned earlier, and often when of is used between two nouns.

Key Points

ExampleArticlesReason
the Indus, the longest river in Pakistanthe, the, no articleriver name and superlative; country name takes none
The capital of Pakistan is IslamabadThe, no article, no articleparticular thing with of; names take none
an orange, an apple, a bananaan, an, avowel sounds take an; banana takes a
the more you exercise, the better your healththe, thetwo comparative degrees together
The Chinese, a road, the Chinese borderThe, a, thenationality/community and a particular border
An intelligent person; many peopleAn, no articlevowel sound; plural people in general takes none

Remember

No article is needed in many places: children go to school at the age of five (no article, no article, the); studying geography in general takes no article, but the geography of the United Arab Emirates takes the. In the lion story, five blanks need no article, including started thinking, upsetting his stomach, given him bananas, What nonsense, and your own country.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'I know that ___ Indus is ___ longest river in ___ Pakistan.'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the, the, no article, because the is used before river names and superlatives, but not before Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Complete: '___ capital of ___ Pakistan is ___ Islamabad.'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is The, no article, no article, because capital is a particular thing while Pakistan and Islamabad are names.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'eating ___ orange, ___ apple and ___ banana'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is an, an, a, because orange and apple begin with vowel sounds and banana begins with a consonant sound.

mcqs.q: Complete: '___ more you exercise, ___ better your health.'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the, the, because the is used when two comparative degrees are used together.

mcqs.q: Complete: '___ Chinese are helping ___ Pakistanis to build ___ road.'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is The, no article, a, because the is used before a community, Pakistanis takes none here, and road is a countable singular.

mcqs.q: Complete: '___ intelligent person always thinks before speaking, but many ___ people...'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is An, no article, because intelligent begins with a vowel sound and people in general takes no article.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'children ___ go to ___ school at ___ age of five.'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is no article, no article, the, as given for this sentence in the articles exercise.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'studying ___ geography, and in particular ___ geography of ___ United Arab Emirates.'
mcqs.why: The correct answer is no article, the, the, because a subject in general takes none but a particular geography with of takes the.

mcqs.q: With which nouns are a / an used?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is countable singular nouns, because the book says a and an are used with countable singular nouns.

mcqs.q: In the lion story, which phrase needs no article before it?
options: Your own country (in: better to be a lion in your own country)
mcqs.why: The correct answer is your own country, one of the five blanks in the lion story where no article is needed.

lessons.title: Writing: Informal Emails and Compare and Contrast Essay
lessons.notes_html:
Informal Emails

Informal emails are written to family, friends and colleagues. Emails are different from letters: they have To, Cc and Subject lines, are usually brief and to the point, and use informal language, with no postal address or date.

EmailSent bySent toCcSubject
1IqbalFareed KhanSohail Alisports day practice
2KapoorAdilnonemaths homework
3AdilSunil Kapoornonemaths homework
4Nadiasix peopleSaira Guddu and Mahnaz Munniwedding invitation

The four emails do not begin or end in the same manner, and their language differs: some are more formal (Dear Adil, Regards) and some very informal (Bye, See you on Saturday). The subject line carries a short phrase naming the topic. Model request email: To a friend, Subject: borrow your science notes - Dear Sara, I hope you are well. I was absent yesterday and missed the science lesson. Could you please lend me your science notes for one day? I will return them tomorrow. Thanks. Ali.

Compare and Contrast Essay

The model essay is Autumn versus Spring. The introduction names both seasons, says both are celebrated in many parts of the world, and then points to differences with However. Body paragraph 1 describes spring: rebirth, new leaves and buds, animals becoming active, people preparing for summer. Body paragraph 2 describes autumn with on the other hand: leaves turning yellow, brown and red and falling, trees becoming barren, animals hoarding food, people hurrying home and harvesting. The conclusion begins with All in all: spring signals winter's end and a new beginning; autumn signals summer's end and more rest.

  • Similarity words: both, celebrated, various ways.
  • Difference words: However, on the other hand, instead of, All in all.
  • Essay topics given: Summer and Winter; Pet and wild animals; City and village life; Good neighbours and bad neighbours.

Remember

For City and Village Life: city life is fast with facilities but noise and pollution; village life is slow and peaceful with fresh air but often lacks good schools, hospitals and jobs.

mcqs.q: To whom are informal emails written?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is family, friends and colleagues, the people to whom informal emails are written in the book.

mcqs.q: How are emails usually written?
options: Long, with a postal address and date
Brief and to the point, in informal language
mcqs.why: The correct answer is brief and to the point in informal language, which is how the book describes emails.

mcqs.q: What is written in the subject line of an email?
options: A short phrase naming the topic
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a short phrase naming the topic, which is what the subject line carries in the model emails.

mcqs.q: Email 1 was sent by Iqbal to Fareed Khan. What was its subject?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is sports day practice, the subject of Email 1 sent by Iqbal to Fareed Khan.

mcqs.q: Email 4, the wedding invitation, was sent by whom?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Nadia, who sent Email 4, the wedding invitation, to six people.

mcqs.q: Do all four model emails begin and end in the same manner?
options: Yes, all begin and end identically
No, their beginnings and endings differ
Only the endings are the same
Only the beginnings are the same
mcqs.why: The correct answer is no, because the beginnings differ and the endings differ across the four model emails.

mcqs.q: In the Autumn versus Spring essay, what does the introduction do?
options: Names both seasons, notes both are celebrated, then points to differences with However
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it names both seasons, says both are celebrated, and then points to differences with However.

mcqs.q: Which words show difference in the essay?
options: However, on the other hand, instead of
mcqs.why: The correct answer is However, on the other hand and instead of, which are the words showing differences in the essay.

mcqs.q: How does the conclusion of the essay begin?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is All in all, the phrase with which the concluding paragraph of the essay begins.

mcqs.q: In body paragraph 2, what do animals do in autumn?
options: They grow new leaves and buds
mcqs.why: The correct answer is they hoard food, because in autumn animals start hoarding their food in preparation for winter.

lessons.title: Study Skills: Analysing Information in a Bar/Line Graph
lessons.notes_html:
About the Graphs

Study Skills teaches analysing information given in a bar / line graph. Read the title, the labels, which bar stands for whom, and the numbers on each bar, then supply information, find differences, and state what the graph tells us. This section is for acquiring additional language skills and is not to be formally assessed.

Graph 1: Men versus Women in Management Positions

PositionWomenMen
Executive Management57%52%
Senior Manager56%50%
Middle Manager55%51%

Women are ahead at all three levels, so in no position are there more men. Differences: Senior Manager 6%, Executive Management 5%, Middle Manager 4%. The highest number of women and of men is at Executive Management; the lowest women at Middle Manager (55%) and lowest men at Senior Manager (50%). Capability is not decided by gender.

Graph 2: Educational Levels and Employment Rates

Education levelUnemployed menUnemployed women
Less than a high school diploma15.0%14.6%
High school graduates11.3%9.0%
Some college or Associate degree9.0%7.8%

The education graph tells us: higher education goes with lower unemployment - the more educated people are, the less likely they are to be unemployed.

mcqs.q: In the management graph, what percentage of women are Senior Managers?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 56 percent, the percentage of women in the Senior Manager position in the graph.

mcqs.q: What percentage of women are in Executive Management?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 57 percent, the highest percentage of women, at Executive Management level.

mcqs.q: What percentage of men are Middle Managers?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 51 percent, the percentage of men in the Middle Manager position in the graph.

mcqs.q: How much difference is there between men and women at Senior Manager level?

mcqs.q: In which management position are there more men than women?
options: In no position - women are ahead at all three levels
mcqs.why: The correct answer is no position, because women hold a higher percentage at all three management levels.

mcqs.q: What percentage of unemployed men have less than a high school diploma?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 15.0 percent, the unemployment figure for men with less than a high school diploma.

mcqs.q: What percentage of unemployed women have a Bachelor's degree or more?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 4.7 percent, the lowest unemployment figure for women, at Bachelor's degree or more level.

mcqs.q: How much difference is there between unemployed men and women who are High School graduates?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2.3 percent, because 11.3 percent men minus 9.0 percent women gives 2.3.

mcqs.q: What percentage of unemployed men have some college or an Associate degree?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 9.0 percent, the unemployment figure for men with some college or an Associate degree.

mcqs.q: What does the education graph tell us?

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: The Great Visionaries
lessons.notes_html:
Summary

This reading lesson is about two great visionaries, Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Allama Muhammad Iqbal. A visionary is a person who can think about or plan the future with imagination and wisdom. The book web lists visionary qualities such as vision, clear goals, clear communication, integrity, inspiration, encouragement, support, recognition, a good example, focus on team interests and needs, stimulating work and expecting the best.

About the Text

The Quaid's message was Unity, Faith and Discipline, and his greatest achievement was the creation of Pakistan. He left the Congress, joined the Muslim League, and wanted Pakistan to be a state of equal citizens with justice and merit. Allama Iqbal was a poet, professor of Arabic, barrister and Ph.D. In his Allahabad address in 1930 he demanded a separate Muslim state, which led to the Pakistan Resolution in 1940 and the creation of Pakistan in 1947. He died in 1938 and advised Muslims to remain true to Islam.

Key Points

  • Quaid-e-Azam qualities: dynamic, determined, steadfast, tolerant, just and impartial.
  • His vision: equal rights for all citizens, no discrimination, justice and merit prevailing.
  • Iqbal academic record: M.A., Professor of Arabic at Oriental College Lahore in 1899, law degree from London in 1905, barrister, Ph.D. from Munich University on Persian philosophy in 1908.
  • Iqbal dream: Punjab, North West Frontier Province, Sindh and Baluchistan united under a single Muslim state.
  • Famous words of the Quaid on 11 August 1947 in the Constituent Assembly: citizens are free to go to temples, mosques or any other place of worship, and all are equal citizens of one State.

Vocabulary

WordMeaning
dynamicactive and energetic
steadfastnessfirmness, not giving up
acumensharpness of judgement
proponentsupporter
aspirationshopes and ambitions
envisionedimagined, pictured in the mind
discriminationunfair treatment
impartialityfairness, not favouring any side
versatileable to do many things well
homagerespect and honour shown publicly

Remember

Students collected information by topic: Tahira and Huma on the personality and achievements of the Quaid, Farheen on the political acumen and contribution of Allama Iqbal, Huma on the Quaid aspirations, Tahira on Iqbal aspirations and on the Quaid political acumen, and Lubna on the personality and achievements of Allama Iqbal. Hindu leaders like Gokhale and Sarojini Naidu called the Quaid the best Ambassador of Hindu Muslim Unity because of his tolerance.

About the Activity

This Listening and Speaking section focuses on asking and responding to questions of academic nature. The class holds a press conference. Students work in groups of eight or ten students, and each group of ten conducts its own press conference.

Roles

  • Three or four students in each group represent one ministry. They are the panellists.
  • Five or six students are reporters from the media, both press and television.
  • Students from the other groups are the audience, and they can also ask questions from the panellists.

Ministries in the Book

How to Do It

The students representing the ministry will all say one thing that their ministry is doing or plans to do. Each group should brainstorm and decide what the panellists will say, what questions the reporters will ask, and what answers will be given. lessons.title: Language Practice: Change the Voice
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar Rules

In this fluency game you change the voice of a sentence without changing the meaning. The passive verb is formed as be plus past participle, for example is cleaned and were given. For the future, use will plus be plus past participle, for example will be given and will be told. The class divides into Group A and Group B. Each group writes a list of 8 to 10 sentences containing active and passive sentences. One group says a sentence and the other group changes its voice and says it out loud.

Book Example

Group A: Aliya ate the grapes. Group B: The grapes were eaten by Aliya. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence, and the tense stays the same.

Tense Table from the Book

TenseActivePassive
Present simplegiveis given
Present continuousis givingis being given
Present perfecthas givenhas been given
Past simplegavewas given
Past continuouswas givingwas being given
Past perfecthad givenhad been given

More Model Pairs

  • The teacher checks our homework - Our homework is checked by the teacher.
  • The students are writing a letter - A letter is being written by the students.
  • She has finished her work - Her work has been finished by her.
  • They will build a new school - A new school will be built by them.
  • The cat drank the milk - The milk was drunk by the cat.

Remember

The same passive pattern completes the earthquake news report and Samina report to the police: was damaged, were broken, were destroyed, were disrupted, are expected, are being rushed, was emptied and were taken away.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is A new school will be built by them, because future passive is will be plus past participle built.

lessons.title: Language Practice: Prefixes
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Prefix?

We sometimes add a pair or a group of letters at the beginning of a word to add something to the meaning of a word. These are called prefixes. Examples from the book: re plus try makes retry, re plus group makes regroup, mis plus spell makes misspell, and mis plus trust makes mistrust. A prefix can also form the opposite of a word: dis plus join makes disjoin, dis plus allow makes disallow, un plus tidy makes untidy, and un plus clear makes unclear.

Prefix re - Again

WordUse in the Book
reclaimThe government is trying to reclaim land from the sea in Karachi.
reprintThe company had to reprint this book three times.
reapplyI advised my friend to reapply for a teaching position.
retellMy father likes to retell his childhood stories to his grandchildren.
rearrangeSaira and Khalida decided to rearrange the furniture in their room.
redoThe teacher told the class to redo the exercise.

Prefix mis - Wrongly

  • misbehave - When children misbehave they are often punished by their parents.
  • misplace - My brothers always misplace their mobile phones.
  • mismatch - There is a mismatch between their income and expenditure.
  • misunderstand - Many people misunderstand their leader message.
  • mistreat - It is not right to mistreat servants.

Prefix inter - Between

  • intercity - The intercity bus service is very good in some countries.
  • international - There is more international travel today than about fifty years ago.
  • interpersonal - For success in any work good interpersonal skills are needed.
  • interdependent - The quality of goods and their price are interdependent.
  • Interfaith - Interfaith understanding is very important for peace in the world.

options: A pair or group of letters added at the beginning of a word to add to its meaning
Letters added at the end of a word
mcqs.why: The correct answer is letters added at the beginning of a word, because the book defines prefixes as a pair or group of letters added at the beginning.

lessons.title: Writing: Paraphrasing a Poem and Application
lessons.notes_html:
Paraphrasing a Poem - The Four Rs

Paraphrasing can help you understand poetry well. The Four Rs of Paraphrasing are: Reword - replace words and phrases with synonyms wherever you can. Rearrange - rearrange words within stanzas or couplets to make proper sentences; you can even rearrange the ideas presented within stanzas or couplets. Realize - realize that some words and phrases, such as names, dates and titles, cannot be changed, but you can present them differently in your paraphrase. Recheck - check to see that the paraphrase conveys the same meaning as the poem.

Vocabulary of A Child's Invocation

WordMeaning
longinga strong desire
supplicationa humble prayer or request
sparklingshining brightly
attainachieve, reach
elegancegrace and beauty
motha night insect like a butterfly
supportivegiving help and encouragement
sufferingpain, hardship

Paraphrase in a Paragraph

The child prays that his deep desire may come to his lips as his prayer. He asks Allah that his life may be like a candle, so that through his light the world's darkness may disappear and every place may sparkle with his light. He prays that through him his homeland may attain elegance, just as a garden attains elegance through flowers. He prays that, like a moth, his life may love the lamp of knowledge, and that supporting the poor and loving the old and the suffering may be his way of life. Finally, he asks God to protect him from evil ways and to show him the path leading to good ways. The poem is a translation of Allama Iqbal poem Lab pay ati hai dua.

How to Write an Application

The book sample has five labelled parts: 1. The address of the person to whom the letter is written. 2. Greetings or Salutation: Dear followed by the person position or name. 3. Closing: words like sincerely, yours truly, thank you, written with a capital letter and followed by a comma. 4. The body of the letter: stating the purpose clearly, along with the request, suggestion, etc. 5. Signature followed by the name of the writer and his or her position. Sample body: I shall not be able to attend school today because I am suffering from high fever. Kindly allow me a day leave. I shall be obliged. Model application to the Principal: We, the students of Class IX, request you to allow our class to visit the Karachi Museum. The visit will help us learn about the history and culture of our country in a practical way. We will go with our class teacher and return before the school closes. We shall be very grateful for your permission. After writing, exchange your paper with your partner, read each other work, give feedback, make changes if needed, and rewrite the corrected application in your notebook.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is replace words and phrases with synonyms, because Reword is the first of the Four Rs defined on page 94.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is that names, dates and titles cannot be changed, because Realize teaches that such words stay, though presented differently.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is check that the paraphrase conveys the same meaning as the poem, because Recheck is the final step of the Four Rs.

options: Words like sincerely, yours truly, thank you, with a capital letter and followed by a comma

lessons.title: Study Skills: Listening for Information
lessons.notes_html:
About Listening for Information

We are listening all the time, but for academic purposes we need specialized focused skills. This Study Skills section gives a small activity for focused listening: a story followed by exercises to check how well you have listened. Students first read the questions silently, then listen to the story when the teacher reads it. They are not allowed to ask questions when the story is being read. The teacher reads the story three times, and each time students do a different task, listening carefully because for each task the story is read only once.

The Fox and the Stork - Story Summary

Long ago, there was a stork and his friend the fox. They lived in a jungle. The fox was famous for being cunning. The stork, on the other hand, was known for being kind and gentle. One day the fox invited the stork for dinner and served him soup in a dish. The stork was unable to have the soup because the soup was thinly spread out in the dish, so he could not manage it with his long beak. He had to return home hungry. Next week, the stork invited the fox for dinner and served fish in a narrow vase. The fox could not reach the fish at the bottom of the narrow vase and had to return home hungry. This is called tit for tat: he did to the fox what the fox had done to him.

Spider Webs

PointFoxStork
Famous forbeing cunningbeing kind and gentle
Invitedthe storkthe fox
Mealsoupfish
Served ina disha narrow vase
Resultstork went home hungryfox went home hungry

Key Message

The stork had other choices: he could have served the fox in a utensil suitable for him and set an example of true hospitality, or invited other animals too and served each their favourite food in suitable utensils. The key message is that we should not follow tit for tat. God tells us to replace the bad with the good. Even if someone does something bad to us, we should be good to them, and this will make the world a better place.
